explanation: Fires on a word-piece or token inside a multi-token technical term or proper name where the next pieces are highly predictable (neuro|logic, tam|pons, phosph|ol|ipids, scala tym|pani, Obstetrics & G|ynecology, RT-|PCR, Par|ity, Copyright (c|)). Topics vary widely. Ordinary prose words give only weak activation.

Fires on the first sub-word piece of a word that is split into pieces, most often a capital or lowercase P/G/R-type onset (R|otten, gl|omerular, P|ondering, p|angs, P|DB, P|appas, P|wC, dig|unakan). The cue is the token being the start of a word that continues. Strongest at a name or term onset that follows a space, weak on ordinary whole words.

Fires on function words and grammar words in formal or boilerplate phrasing where a fixed continuation is expected ('referred to', 'designed for/to be', 'considered to', 'the following', 'Description of the Related Art', 'banned from use in'). Also fires on field-label words such as 'description:' and 'Resolution'. The token matters less than its being part of a set expression, and plain prose is weak.

Fires mostly on a token that completes a fixed collocation, above all 'to' in 'referred to', 'with respect to', 'dedication to' and 'on' in 'effect on'. It also fires on the remaining pieces of compound or code words (Front|end, current|URL, Comb|obox, cath|ode, em|uls|ifying). Strongest on 'referred [to]'.

Fires on a token at a point where a fixed phrase or contrast continues, especially in license or disclaimer boilerplate ('web site', 'License:', 'Software or, alternatively', 'Contributor(s)', 'for more information', 'and not Gamasutra') and in contrastive conversational clauses ('but not on IE7', ', or', ', but', 'had they not'). This is a broad, diffuse continuation-in-boilerplate pattern.

Fires on an opening parenthesis ' (' that starts a parenthetical aside, abbreviation, count or definition right after a noun phrase ('documentation files (the "Software")', 'ten patients (nine men', 'DAMAGES (INCLUDING', 'likelihood ratio (LR)'). It peaks in license boilerplate and narrative asides. Closing parentheses and other tokens are weak.

Fires on deictic or emphatic words in casual, spoken-style narration that point at a place or moment, mainly 'right' ('right there', 'right now', 'That's right', 'Right?') plus 'over there', 'Look at', 'up there' and 'here'. It needs a conversational context and is near zero in formal text.

Fires mostly on a loop variable after 'for' in code ('for i in', 'for (var i'). It also fires on 'a' in quantity phrases ('quite a', 'from a half-mile') and on single characters or digits inside identifiers, acronyms and numbers (IP|N, ch|p, IV|I|AT, 6|6%, 11|0). Strongest on 'for [i]'.

Fires mainly on the decimal point inside a number (23[.]3%, 12[.]9 inches, 9[.]3.0, 1.14-3[.]17). A second, weaker group is adjectives that start a fixed technical compound ('organic synthesis/solvent', 'central nervous system', 'directional selection', 'primary DNA sequence').

Fires on a token that introduces the next item in a list of parameters or conjuncts: commas between function arguments, 'typename' in template lists, '@param', and 'and'/'with'/'a' joining a coordinated noun phrase ('two arrays and [an] integer'). It also fires weakly on 'v.' in case captions. Strongest when it starts the second item of a parameter or argument list.

Fires on a token right after a number or code value, mainly units and measure words ('10 [percent]', '80 [mM]', '28.3[%]', '0[px]', 'minutes [ago]') and figure reference numerals ('screw [2]24', 'envelope [3]'). It also fires on assorted pieces of names and terms (Battle|front, A|HL, E|UV, Bho|jp|uri). Broad and somewhat mixed.

Fires on gerund or present-participle '-ing' forms, either a whole word ('powering', 'licensing', 'sealing', 'calling', 'stirring', 'stumbling') or an '-ing' suffix piece (cough|ing, taxi|ing, stom|ping), especially when used as a modifier or nominal before a noun. Other words are weak.

Fires on the last sub-word piece that completes a word or fixed term, notably 'CIRCU[IT]' in court headers, plus 'precis[aram]', 'method [stub]', 'travis-ci[.org]' and 'hyperbar[ic]'. It also fires on '=' in math definitions like 'Let s(w) ='. Mixed across code, legal and science text.

Fires on commas that separate items in a list of coordinated adjectives or nouns ('personal, academic, and professional', 'mental, physical', 'DIRECT, INDIRECT') and on commas in dates ('March 12, 13', 'February 28, 196x') and parameter lists. Commas that end clauses fire weakly.

Fires on a word that refers back to a task, action or effort, mostly a pro-form or generic noun: 'do' / 'done' / 'do this' / 'the same thing' / 'job' / 'process' / 'effort' / 'cost' / 'steps', as in 'what I am attempting above' or 'what I have done'. Words in other roles are weak.

Fires on a scattering of unrelated tokens: an OID digit, 'Summer' in 'the YEAR Summer Olympics', 'ins' in 'topological insulators', CSS 'content:', shell 'if [' tests, 'derive', and 'World' in 'World Aquatics Championships'. The clearest repeating item is 'Summer' after an Olympic year.

Fires on word fragments inside text where the word is split into pieces: foreign-language words (napolitan|oy, turval|is), legal citations and formatting (O R D E R, app|elle|e, rem|anded, est|oppel, J|UD|GMENT) and chemical or gene abbreviations (E|PO, HLA-C, M|ny). These are mostly low-frequency pieces with no shared meaning.

Fires on a broad mix of tokens with no clear common feature: URL slashes and domains, markdown table pipes, code identifiers, and prose words in fixed phrases ('few and far between', 'all over the country', 'not many guys', 'President of the Society'). No single context dominates.

Fires on the second token of a highly predictable fixed multi-token unit: 'look [like]', 'President [Obama]', 'George [Washington]', 'West [Virginia]', 'Long [Island]', 'College/Institute [of]', '/[usr]/bin', 'ASP[.NET]', '$this[->]'. Strength depends on how strongly the preceding context fixes this token.

Fires on tokens inside formulaic, structured text such as code import lists ('"errors"', 'os', '.h', newlines after an import), doc headers ('One of the [following] permissions'), 'Code Generator', court headers ('SUMMARY ORDER') and citation spacing. The common thread is boilerplate or structured lists. The examples are heterogeneous.

Fires on tokens in web-page or document metadata and UI boilerplate: newlines after header fields ('Released', 'Menu', email 'To:'), 'Shares', 'Posted:', 'Share this post', 'special reports', '-share', 'shortcut icon', and also code or config keywords ('fluidPage', 'compile', '-c'). It also fires on some technical compounds (Rankine Cycle, Plant cell). Mostly a page-chrome / boilerplate detector with mixed extras.
